Unit 3 check

About 20 minutes: one fresh question for each part of every outcome of Unit 3, plus two from earlier units to keep them sharp. It is not graded and only you see it.

An outcome becomes Secure when you have answered a question on each of its parts right first time, without a hint or the solution, here in this check. When all 5 are secure you are ready to try Canvas Quiz 3 (due Sun 1 Nov). Already know this material? Take the check before the lessons and skip what is secure.

Form A

3a multiply matrices and matrix × vector by hand and with @, and decide when a product is defined.

Your answerMatrix × vector3a

A=(4333)\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 \end{pmatrix}A=(43​33​) and x=(−23)\mathbf{x} = \begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}x=(−23​). What is the second component of Ax\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}Ax?

You added the pairs. Multiply each entry of the row by the matching component of x\mathbf{x}x, then add the products.
That is only one product. Row 2 has 2 entries: multiply each by the matching component of x\mathbf{x}x and add them all.
The second component uses row 2 of A\mathbf{A}A, which is (3,3)(3, 3)(3,3).
Multiply that row by x\mathbf{x}x pair by pair and add: a dot product.
Solution

Row 2 of A\mathbf{A}A times x\mathbf{x}x: (3)(−2)+(3)(3)=3(3)(-2) + (3)(3) = 3(3)(−2)+(3)(3)=3.

Review: Unit 3 · Lesson 3.1 · A matrix and its shape

Your answerAn entry of a matrix product (2×2, 3×3)3a

A=(4−1−21)\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & -1 \\ -2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}A=(4−2​−11​) and B=(022131)\mathbf{B} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}B=(01​23​21​). What is the entry in row 1, column 1 of AB\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}AB?

You added the pairs. Multiply each pair, then add the products.
Take row 1 of A\mathbf{A}A and column 1 of B\mathbf{B}B.
Multiply them pair by pair, then add.
Solution

Row 1 of A\mathbf{A}A is (4,−1)(4, -1)(4,−1) and column 1 of B\mathbf{B}B is (0,1)(0, 1)(0,1): (4)(0)+(−1)(1)=−1(4)(0) + (-1)(1) = -1(4)(0)+(−1)(1)=−1.

Review: Unit 3 · Lesson 3.1 · Matrix times matrix

ChooseWhen is a product defined? Shapes, @ and *3a

A\mathbf{A}A is a 2×52 \times 52×5 matrix and B\mathbf{B}B is a 5×55 \times 55×5 matrix. What is the shape of AB\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}AB?

2×52 \times 52×5
The inner numbers match (5 and 5), and the shape comes from the outer numbers: 2 rows from A\mathbf{A}A, 5 columns from B\mathbf{B}B.
5×55 \times 55×5
Those are the inner numbers. They must match for the product to exist; the shape of the result comes from the outer numbers.
5×25 \times 25×2
Rows come from the first matrix and columns from the second: 2×52 \times 52×5, not the other way round.
Not defined
A\mathbf{A}A has 5 columns and B\mathbf{B}B has 5 rows. They match, so AB\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}AB exists.

3b describe a 2×2 matrix as a transformation of the plane and recognise an eigenvector as a direction that is only stretched.

ChooseThe matrix of a transformation3b

Which matrix stretches the plane horizontally by a factor of 4?

(4001)\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}(40​01​)
The columns are the images of the basis vectors: (1,0)↦(4,0)(1, 0) \mapsto (4, 0)(1,0)↦(4,0) and (0,1)↦(0,1)(0, 1) \mapsto (0, 1)(0,1)↦(0,1).
(0110)\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}(01​10​)
This matrix sends (1,0)↦(0,1)(1, 0) \mapsto (0, 1)(1,0)↦(0,1) and (0,1)↦(1,0)(0, 1) \mapsto (1, 0)(0,1)↦(1,0): it reflects every point in the line y=xy = xy=x.
(0−110)\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}(01​−10​)
This matrix sends (1,0)↦(0,1)(1, 0) \mapsto (0, 1)(1,0)↦(0,1) and (0,1)↦(−1,0)(0, 1) \mapsto (-1, 0)(0,1)↦(−1,0): it rotates the plane 90° anticlockwise about the origin.
(−1001)\begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}(−10​01​)
This matrix sends (1,0)↦(−1,0)(1, 0) \mapsto (-1, 0)(1,0)↦(−1,0) and (0,1)↦(0,1)(0, 1) \mapsto (0, 1)(0,1)↦(0,1): it reflects every point in the yyy-axis.
ChooseSpot an eigenvector3b

Which of these vectors is an eigenvector of A=(50−24)\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}A=(5−2​04​)?

(1,−2)(1, -2)(1,−2)
For v=(1,−2)\mathbf{v} = (1, -2)v=(1,−2), Av=(5,−10)\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} = (5, -10)Av=(5,−10), which is 5×(1,−2)5 \times (1, -2)5×(1,−2): it stays on the same line through the origin, only stretched (or flipped).
(5,−2)(5, -2)(5,−2)
That is a column of A\mathbf{A}A: where a basis vector goes, not an eigenvector. For w=(5,−2)\mathbf{w} = (5, -2)w=(5,−2), Aw=(25,−18)\mathbf{A}\mathbf{w} = (25, -18)Aw=(25,−18), which is not a multiple of w\mathbf{w}w: the direction changes.
(1,1)(1, 1)(1,1)
For w=(1,1)\mathbf{w} = (1, 1)w=(1,1), Aw=(5,2)\mathbf{A}\mathbf{w} = (5, 2)Aw=(5,2), which is not a multiple of w\mathbf{w}w: the direction changes.
(1,−1)(1, -1)(1,−1)
For w=(1,−1)\mathbf{w} = (1, -1)w=(1,−1), Aw=(5,−6)\mathbf{A}\mathbf{w} = (5, -6)Aw=(5,−6), which is not a multiple of w\mathbf{w}w: the direction changes.

3c select, filter and sort rows and columns of a DataFrame.

ChooseSelect rows and columns3c

What does the last line print?

import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "station": ["Ely", "Rye", "Hoy", "Wye", "Bude"],
    "wind": [12, 10, 52, 34, 43],
    "sun": [2, 5, 7, 3, 7],
})
print(df["wind"].shape)
(5,)
Single brackets give one column as a Series, which has one dimension: (rows,).
(5, 1)
df["..."] with one name gives a Series, not a DataFrame: its shape has one number.
(1, 5)
Rows come first in a shape, and a column runs down the rows.
(5, 3)
Only the selected column is kept, not the whole table.
ChooseFilter rows3c

What does the last line print?

import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "station": ["Rye", "Hoy", "Kew", "Ely", "Bude", "Looe"],
    "wind": [8, 24, 40, 11, 48, 45],
    "sun": [7, 4, 4, 10, 10, 5],
})
print(df[df["wind"] > 17].shape)
(4, 3)
4 rows have wind above 17; all 3 columns are kept. .shape is (rows, columns).
(6, 3)
A filter keeps only the rows where the condition is True: 4 of the 6.
(3, 4)
.shape gives rows first, then columns.
(4,)
A DataFrame's shape always has two numbers, rows and columns. Only a single column (a Series) has a shape like (k,).
ChooseSort rows3c

What does the last line print?

import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "student": ["Gus", "Chen", "Femi", "Eli", "Asha", "Ben"],
    "score": [77, 41, 47, 44, 45, 62],
    "hours": [12, 12, 1, 1, 5, 11],
})
print(df.sort_values("score").head(2)["student"].tolist())
['Chen', 'Eli']
Sorting puts the smallest score first, and .head(2) keeps the first 2 rows of the sorted table.
['Gus', 'Ben']
sort_values sorts from smallest to largest by default.
['Gus', 'Chen']
.head(2) comes after the sort, so it keeps the first 2 rows of the sorted table, not of the original one.
['Asha', 'Ben']
The rows are sorted by score, not by student: alphabetical order plays no part.

3d describe a distribution's shape, standardise values (z-scores) and use the 68–95–99.7 rule.

ChooseDescribe a distribution's shape3d

The histogram shows 560 waiting times at a GP surgery. Which description fits it best?

Unimodal and roughly symmetric (bell-shaped): a normal model could describe it
One peak in the middle, and the two sides mirror each other with tails thinning out: a bell shape.
Unimodal and right-skewed: the long tail is towards large values, so the mean is above the median
A right skew has a long tail towards large values; this histogram does not.
Unimodal and left-skewed: the long tail is towards small values, so the mean is below the median
A left skew has a long tail towards small values; this histogram does not.
Bimodal: two peaks, perhaps two groups mixed together, so one normal curve would not fit
Count the peaks: this histogram has only one.
Your answerz-scores3d

The reaction times in a lab test have mean 283 ms and standard deviation 44 ms. Which value has a z-score of −1.2-1.2−1.2? Give the value in ms.

Check the sign: a negative z-score is below the mean, a positive one above it.
zzz counts standard deviations: move z×s=−1.2×44z \times s = -1.2 \times 44z×s=−1.2×44 ms from the mean, not −1.2-1.2−1.2 ms.
That is the distance from the mean. Add it to the mean to get the value.
Rearrange z=(x−xˉ)/sz = (x - \bar{x})/sz=(x−xˉ)/s: x=xˉ+z sx = \bar{x} + z\,sx=xˉ+zs.
Solution

x=283+(−1.2)×44=230.2x = 283 + (-1.2) \times 44 = 230.2x=283+(−1.2)×44=230.2 ms.

Review: Unit 3 · Lesson 3.4 · How many SDs from the mean

Your answerThe 68–95–99.7 rule3d

The heights of adult men in a survey are roughly normal, with mean 176 cm and standard deviation 8 cm. By the 68–95–99.7 rule, what percentage of them are between 168 and 184 cm?

That is the percentage on the other side. Check which side of the value you want.
That is only one side of the mean. Within 1 SD on both sides is 68%.
That is within 2 SDs.
Turn the value(s) into SDs from the mean first.
Sketch the curve: 34% between the mean and 1 SD on each side, 13.5% between 1 and 2 SDs, 2.5% beyond 2 SDs on each side.
Solution

xˉ−1s=168\bar{x} - 1s = 168xˉ−1s=168 and xˉ+1s=184\bar{x} + 1s = 184xˉ+1s=184. Adding the pieces of the curve gives 68%.

3e simulate uniform and normal data and compare the histogram with the model curve.

ChooseSimulate uniform and normal data3e

rng is a NumPy random generator, made with rng = np.random.default_rng(7). Which line simulates 2000 values from a normal distribution with mean 100 and variance 4?

rng.normal(100, 2, size=2000)
normal(mean, sd, size=n), and the SD is 2 (the square root of the variance 4).
rng.normal(100, 4, size=2000)
The second argument is the standard deviation: the square root of the variance, 4=2\sqrt{4} = 24​=2.
rng.normal(4, 100, size=2000)
The mean comes first, then the SD: normal(mean, sd, size=n).
rng.normal(100, 2)
Without size, this gives a single number, not 2000 values.
ChooseCompare a histogram with the model3e

This code simulates data and draws a histogram with a normal model curve on top (picture below). rng, np, plt and stats (from SciPy) are already set up. Which statement is right?

x = rng.normal(50, 6, size=2000)
plt.hist(x, bins=30, density=True)
grid = np.linspace(26, 74, 200)
plt.plot(grid, stats.norm.pdf(grid, 50, 6))
plt.show()
Nothing is wrong: the bars differ from the curve only by random variation in the sample
The code and the picture agree: bars and curve are on the same scale, centred together, with the same spread.
The histogram shows counts, not densities: add density=True
The code already has density=True: the bars are on the density scale, like the curve.
The mean and the SD are swapped in the curve
The curve's first number, 50, is the mean used for the data, and its second, 6, is the SD.
The data are not normal, so no normal curve can fit
The data come from rng.normal, so they are normal. A mismatch must come from how the picture was drawn.

The reaction times in a lab test are roughly normal, with mean 262 ms and standard deviation 42 ms. By the 68–95–99.7 rule, what percentage of them are between 304 and 346 ms?

That is 95% − 68%, which covers both sides. One side is half of it.
That starts at the mean. Start at 1 SD above it: 47.5% − 34%.
That is the percentage on the other side. Check which side of the value you want.
Turn the value(s) into SDs from the mean first.

xˉ+1s=304\bar{x} + 1s = 304xˉ+1s=304 and xˉ+2s=346\bar{x} + 2s = 346xˉ+2s=346. Adding the pieces of the curve gives 13.5%.

rng.uniform(5, 35, size=1000)
uniform(low, high, size=n): 1000 values spread evenly between 5 and 35.
rng.integers(5, 35, size=1000)
integers gives whole numbers only (and never 35 itself), not a continuous uniform distribution.

That is a normal distribution (with mean 5 and SD 35), not a uniform one.

When is a product defined? Shapes, @ and *

Taught in Lesson 3.1 · Matrices — tables you can multiply.

Choose3a

A\mathbf{A}A is a 3×23 \times 23×2 matrix and B\mathbf{B}B is a 4×24 \times 24×2 matrix. What is the shape of AB\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}AB?

Not defined
A\mathbf{A}A has 2 columns but B\mathbf{B}B has 4 rows. Each entry of AB\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}AB pairs a row of A\mathbf{A}A (2 numbers) with a column of B\mathbf{B}B (4 numbers), so these must be equal.
3×23 \times 23×2
The outer numbers give the shape only when the inner numbers match. Here A\mathbf{A}A has 2 columns but B\mathbf{B}B has 4 rows.
2×32 \times 32×3
The order of the factors matters, and here the inner numbers do not even match.
2×42 \times 42×4
Those are the inner numbers, 2 and 4. They are different, so the product does not exist.
Choose3a

A\mathbf{A}A is a 4×24 \times 24×2 matrix and B\mathbf{B}B is a 2×32 \times 32×3 matrix. What is the shape of AB\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}AB?

4×34 \times 34×3
The inner numbers match (2 and 2), and the shape comes from the outer numbers: 4 rows from A\mathbf{A}A, 3 columns from B\mathbf{B}B.
2×22 \times 22×2
Those are the inner numbers. They must match for the product to exist; the shape of the result comes from the outer numbers.
3×43 \times 43×4
Rows come from the first matrix and columns from the second: 4×34 \times 34×3, not the other way round.
Not defined
A\mathbf{A}A has 2 columns and B\mathbf{B}B has 2 rows. They match, so AB\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}AB exists.
Choose3a

(5, 3)
A has 5 columns and B has 5 rows, so A @ B works; it has the rows of A (5) and the columns of B (3).
(5, 5)
Those are the inner sizes, which must match. The result takes the outer sizes.
(3, 5)
Rows come from the first factor and columns from the second.
An error (ValueError)
A has 5 columns and B has 5 rows: they match, so @ works.

A has 4 columns and B has 4 rows, so A @ B works; it has the rows of A (3) and the columns of B (4).
(4, 4)
Those are the inner sizes, which must match. The result takes the outer sizes.
(4, 3)
Rows come from the first factor and columns from the second.

A has 4 columns and B has 4 rows: they match, so @ works.

The matrix of a transformation

Taught in Lesson 3.2 · Matrices as transformations.

Choose3b

What does M=(0−110)\mathbf{M} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}M=(01​−10​) do to the plane?

It rotates the plane 90° anticlockwise about the origin
Read the columns: (1,0)↦(0,1)(1, 0) \mapsto (0, 1)(1,0)↦(0,1) and (0,1)↦(−1,0)(0, 1) \mapsto (-1, 0)(0,1)↦(−1,0). That is exactly what this transformation does.
It rotates the plane 90° clockwise about the origin
That is what the matrix with rows and columns swapped does. Read the columns of M\mathbf{M}M: (1,0)↦(0,1)(1, 0) \mapsto (0, 1)(1,0)↦(0,1) and (0,1)↦(−1,0)(0, 1) \mapsto (-1, 0)(0,1)↦(−1,0).
It reflects every point in the line y=xy = xy=x
That transformation sends (1,0)↦(0,1)(1, 0) \mapsto (0, 1)(1,0)↦(0,1) and (0,1)↦(1,0)(0, 1) \mapsto (1, 0)(0,1)↦(1,0). The columns of M\mathbf{M}M say (1,0)↦(0,1)(1, 0) \mapsto (0, 1)(1,0)↦(0,1) and (0,1)↦(−1,0)(0, 1) \mapsto (-1, 0)(0,1)↦(−1,0).
It rotates the plane by 180° about the origin
That transformation sends (1,0)↦(−1,0)(1, 0) \mapsto (-1, 0)(1,0)↦(−1,0) and (0,1)↦(0,−1)(0, 1) \mapsto (0, -1)(0,1)↦(0,−1). The columns of M\mathbf{M}M say (1,0)↦(0,1)(1, 0) \mapsto (0, 1)(1,0)↦(0,1) and (0,1)↦(−1,0)(0, 1) \mapsto (-1, 0)(0,1)↦(−1,0).

The columns are the images of the basis vectors: (1,0)↦(4,0)(1, 0) \mapsto (4, 0)(1,0)↦(4,0) and (0,1)↦(0,4)(0, 1) \mapsto (0, 4)(0,1)↦(0,4).

This matrix sends (1,0)↦(4,0)(1, 0) \mapsto (4, 0)(1,0)↦(4,0) and (0,1)↦(0,1)(0, 1) \mapsto (0, 1)(0,1)↦(0,1): it stretches the plane horizontally by a factor of 4.
Choose3b

What does M=(100−1)\mathbf{M} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}M=(10​0−1​) do to the plane?

It reflects every point in the xxx-axis
Read the columns: (1,0)↦(1,0)(1, 0) \mapsto (1, 0)(1,0)↦(1,0) and (0,1)↦(0,−1)(0, 1) \mapsto (0, -1)(0,1)↦(0,−1). That is exactly what this transformation does.
It rotates the plane 90° anticlockwise about the origin
That transformation sends (1,0)↦(0,1)(1, 0) \mapsto (0, 1)(1,0)↦(0,1) and (0,1)↦(−1,0)(0, 1) \mapsto (-1, 0)(0,1)↦(−1,0). The columns of M\mathbf{M}M say (1,0)↦(1,0)(1, 0) \mapsto (1, 0)(1,0)↦(1,0) and (0,1)↦(0,−1)(0, 1) \mapsto (0, -1)(0,1)↦(0,−1).
It shears the plane horizontally: each point moves right by 4 times its height yyy
That transformation sends (1,0)↦(1,0)(1, 0) \mapsto (1, 0)(1,0)↦(1,0) and (0,1)↦(4,1)(0, 1) \mapsto (4, 1)(0,1)↦(4,1). The columns of M\mathbf{M}M say (1,0)↦(1,0)(1, 0) \mapsto (1, 0)(1,0)↦(1,0) and (0,1)↦(0,−1)(0, 1) \mapsto (0, -1)(0,1)↦(0,−1).
It rotates the plane by 180° about the origin
That transformation sends (1,0)↦(−1,0)(1, 0) \mapsto (-1, 0)(1,0)↦(−1,0) and (0,1)↦(0,−1)(0, 1) \mapsto (0, -1)(0,1)↦(0,−1). The columns of M\mathbf{M}M say (1,0)↦(1,0)(1, 0) \mapsto (1, 0)(1,0)↦(1,0) and (0,1)↦(0,−1)(0, 1) \mapsto (0, -1)(0,1)↦(0,−1).

v=(0,1)\mathbf{v} = (0, 1)v=(0,1) is an eigenvector of A=(4023)\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}A=(42​03​). What is its eigenvalue λ\lambdaλ?

That is a component of Av=(0,3)\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} = (0, 3)Av=(0,3). The eigenvalue is the factor: compare Av\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}Av with v\mathbf{v}v.
That is a diagonal entry of A\mathbf{A}A. Work out Av\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}Av and see what v\mathbf{v}v has been multiplied by.
Check the sign: compare the signs of Av\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}Av and v\mathbf{v}v component by component.
Work out Av\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}Av.
It should be a multiple of v\mathbf{v}v: Av=λv\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}Av=λv. Which multiple?
Solution

Av=(0,3)=3×(0,1)\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} = (0, 3) = 3 \times (0, 1)Av=(0,3)=3×(0,1), so λ=3\lambda = 3λ=3.

Select rows and columns

Taught in Lesson 3.3 · Working with DataFrames.

Choose3c

df is a DataFrame of parkrun results, with columns including minutes and course. Which line gives a table with only the columns course and minutes?

df[["course", "minutes"]]
A list of column names inside the brackets gives a DataFrame with those columns.
df["course", "minutes"]
Without the inner list brackets, pandas looks for one column named by the pair, and raises a KeyError.
df["course"]["minutes"]
df["course"] is one column; asking it for "minutes" looks for a row label, and fails.
df.loc["course", "minutes"]
.loc takes rows first, then columns; there is no row labelled "course".
Choose3c

df is a DataFrame of penguins, with columns including body_mass_g and species. Which line gives the first 4 rows?

df.iloc[:4]
.iloc[:4] takes positions 0 to 3: the first 4 rows.
df.loc[:4]
A .loc slice includes its end label, so this gives 5 rows (labels 0 to 4).
df.iloc[4]
That is a single row, at position 4.
df.iloc[:5]
That gives 5 rows: positions 0 to 4.

['Cork', 'Porto']

Positions count from 0, so position 0 is the first row.

Column position 0 is the first column, "city", not "temp".

df is a DataFrame of parkrun results, with columns including minutes and course. Which line gives the rows where minutes is above 30 and course is "Hatfield"?

df[(df["minutes"] > 30) & (df["course"] == "Hatfield")]
Each condition sits in its own brackets, and & keeps the rows where both are True.
df[df["minutes"] > 30 & df["course"] == "Hatfield"]
Without brackets, & is applied first, to 30 & df["course"], which fails. Put each condition in brackets.
df[(df["minutes"] > 30) | (df["course"] == "Hatfield")]
| means or: it keeps rows where either condition holds.
df[(df["minutes"] > 30) & (df["course"] = "Hatfield")]
A single = assigns; comparing needs ==. This line is a syntax error.

z-scores

The reaction times in a lab test have mean 277 ms and standard deviation 45 ms. What is the z-score of a value of 323 ms? Give 2 decimal places.

That divides by the variance s2=2025s^2 = 2025s2=2025. Divide by the standard deviation, s=45s = 45s=45.
Check the sign: z=(x−xˉ)/sz = (x - \bar{x})/sz=(x−xˉ)/s. A value below the mean has a negative z-score, one above has a positive z-score.
That is the distance from the mean in ms. Divide by the SD to measure it in standard deviations.
Subtract the mean first, then divide by the SD.
z=x−xˉsz = \dfrac{x - \bar{x}}{s}z=sx−xˉ​: how many SDs above (or below) the mean?
Solution

z=323−27745=4645≈1.02z = \dfrac{323 - 277}{45} = \dfrac{46}{45} \approx 1.02z=45323−277​=4546​≈1.02.

Check the sign: a negative z-score is below the mean, a positive one above it.
zzz counts standard deviations: move z×s=2.5×13z \times s = 2.5 \times 13z×s=2.5×13 marks from the mean, not 2.52.52.5 marks.
That is the distance from the mean. Add it to the mean to get the value.
Rearrange z=(x−xˉ)/sz = (x - \bar{x})/sz=(x−xˉ)/s: x=xˉ+z sx = \bar{x} + z\,sx=xˉ+zs.
Solution

x=59+(2.5)×13=91.5x = 59 + (2.5) \times 13 = 91.5x=59+(2.5)×13=91.5 marks.

The 68–95–99.7 rule

Taught in Lesson 3.4 · The shape of data — z-scores and the normal model.

Your answer3d

The heights of adult men in a survey are roughly normal, with mean 175 cm and standard deviation 6 cm. By the 68–95–99.7 rule, what percentage of them are below 163 cm?

That is both tails together. The 5% outside ±2 SD is split equally: 2.5% above, 2.5% below.
That is the percentage above. Below is the other side.
Turn the value(s) into SDs from the mean first.
Sketch the curve: 34% between the mean and 1 SD on each side, 13.5% between 1 and 2 SDs, 2.5% beyond 2 SDs on each side.
Solution

xˉ−2s=163\bar{x} - 2s = 163xˉ−2s=163. Adding the pieces of the curve gives 2.5%.

Review: Unit 3 · Lesson 3.4 · The bell curve and 68–95–99.7

Your answer3d

The reaction times in a lab test are roughly normal, with mean 257 ms and standard deviation 40 ms. By the 68–95–99.7 rule, what percentage of them are between 257 and 297 ms?

That is the percentage on the other side. Check which side of the value you want.
That is both sides of the mean. From the mean up to 1 SD above is half of it.
Turn the value(s) into SDs from the mean first.
Sketch the curve: 34% between the mean and 1 SD on each side, 13.5% between 1 and 2 SDs, 2.5% beyond 2 SDs on each side.
Solution

xˉ=257\bar{x} = 257xˉ=257 and xˉ+1s=297\bar{x} + 1s = 297xˉ+1s=297. Adding the pieces of the curve gives 34%.

The birth weights at a hospital are roughly normal, with mean 3436 g and standard deviation 441 g. By the 68–95–99.7 rule, what percentage of them are between 2554 and 3877 g?

The rule's 68% and 95% are for intervals centred on the mean. Split them in half: 34% on each side within 1 SD, 47.5% within 2 SDs.
The rule's 68% and 95% are for intervals centred on the mean. Split them in half: 34% on each side within 1 SD, 47.5% within 2 SDs.
Adding 68% and 95% counts the middle twice. Use halves: 47.5% + 34%.
That is the percentage on the other side. Check which side of the value you want.
Turn the value(s) into SDs from the mean first.
Sketch the curve: 34% between the mean and 1 SD on each side, 13.5% between 1 and 2 SDs, 2.5% beyond 2 SDs on each side.
Solution

xˉ−2s=2554\bar{x} - 2s = 2554xˉ−2s=2554 and xˉ+1s=3877\bar{x} + 1s = 3877xˉ+1s=3877. Adding the pieces of the curve gives 81.5%.

Simulate uniform and normal data

Taught in Lesson 3.4 · The shape of data — z-scores and the normal model.

Choose3e

rng is a NumPy random generator, made with rng = np.random.default_rng(7). Which line simulates 200 values from a normal distribution with mean 50 and standard deviation 3?

rng.normal(50, 3, size=200)
normal(mean, sd, size=n), and the SD is 3.
rng.normal(3, 50, size=200)
The mean comes first, then the SD: normal(mean, sd, size=n).
rng.normal(50, 9, size=200)
The second argument is the SD, 3. 9 is the variance.
rng.uniform(47, 53, size=200)
That is a flat (uniform) distribution, not a normal one.
Choose3e

rng is a NumPy random generator, made with rng = np.random.default_rng(7). Which line simulates 2000 values from a normal distribution with mean 70 and variance 25?

rng.normal(70, 5, size=2000)
normal(mean, sd, size=n), and the SD is 5 (the square root of the variance 25).
rng.normal(25, 70, size=2000)
The mean comes first, then the SD: normal(mean, sd, size=n).
rng.normal(70, 5)
Without size, this gives a single number, not 2000 values.
rng.normal(70, 12.5, size=2000)
The SD is the square root of the variance, not half of it.
Choose3e

rng is a NumPy random generator, made with rng = np.random.default_rng(7). Which line simulates 2000 values from a normal distribution with mean 10 and standard deviation 6?

rng.normal(10, 6, size=2000)
normal(mean, sd, size=n), and the SD is 6.
rng.normal(6, 10, size=2000)
The mean comes first, then the SD: normal(mean, sd, size=n).
rng.normal(size=2000) + 10
That has SD 1. You would need 6 * rng.normal(size=2000) + 10.
rng.uniform(4, 16, size=2000)
That is a flat (uniform) distribution, not a normal one.

Compare a histogram with the model

Taught in Lesson 3.4 · The shape of data — z-scores and the normal model.

Choose3e

This code simulates data and draws a histogram with a normal model curve on top (picture below). rng, np, plt and stats (from SciPy) are already set up. Which statement is right?

x = rng.normal(50, 5, size=5000)
plt.hist(x, bins=30, density=True)
grid = np.linspace(30, 70, 200)
plt.plot(grid, stats.norm.pdf(grid, 50, 5))
plt.show()
Nothing is wrong: the bars differ from the curve only by random variation in the sample
The code and the picture agree: bars and curve are on the same scale, centred together, with the same spread.
The curve uses the variance where the SD should be, so it is far too wide and flat
The curve's second number is 5, and the data were simulated with SD 5.
The mean and the SD are swapped in the curve
The curve's first number, 50, is the mean used for the data, and its second, 5, is the SD.
The data are not normal, so no normal curve can fit
The data come from rng.normal, so they are normal. A mismatch must come from how the picture was drawn.

The code already has density=True: the bars are on the density scale, like the curve.
The mean and the SD are swapped in the curve
The curve's first number, 50, is the mean used for the data, and its second, 100, is the SD.

Your answer3e

rng.uniform(2, 22, size=n) simulates values from a uniform distribution on [2,22][2, 22][2,22]. What is the height of its density curve? Give a decimal.

That is the width of the interval. The total area must be 1, so the height is 1 divided by the width.
The density is a flat rectangle over the interval, with total area 1.
Solution

Width =22−2=20= 22 - 2 = 20=22−2=20, so the height is 1/20=0.051/20 = 0.051/20=0.05.

Review: Unit 3 · Lesson 3.4 · Simulating from a model

Your answer3e

Values are simulated with rng.uniform(5, 45, size=n). What percentage of them do you expect between 25 and 35?

That is the width of the part you want. Divide by the full width, 40, and turn the fraction into a percentage.
That is the share outside the interval.
The full width is b−a=40b - a = 40b−a=40, not 45.
For a uniform distribution, the share in an interval is its width divided by the full width.
Solution

(35−25)/(45−5)=10/40=0.25(35 - 25)/(45 - 5) = 10/40 = 0.25(35−25)/(45−5)=10/40=0.25, so 25%.

Review: Unit 3 · Lesson 3.4 · Simulating from a model

Your answer3e

You simulate x = rng.uniform(1, 5, size=200). About how many of the 200 values do you expect to lie between 2 and 4?

The full width is b−a=4b - a = 4b−a=4, not 5.
That is the proportion. Multiply by the number of values, 200.
Share in the interval = its width ÷ the full width. Then multiply by the number of values.
Solution

(4−2)/(5−1)=0.5(4 - 2)/(5 - 1) = 0.5(4−2)/(5−1)=0.5, and 0.5×200=1000.5 \times 200 = 1000.5×200=100.
